What could change on the immigration file? To inform readers about the issues that matter to communities, La Converse is publishing a series of articles that detail, theme by theme, what the parties in the race are proposing.

Si l’immigration n’est pas au cœur des d:
Immigration may not be at the heart of the leaders’ debates, but it has been a major issue since the start of the pandemic. Foreign workers have proven to be both the “guardian angels” of a country in a health crisis and an essential cog in the economic recovery. At the same time, they belong to the communities that have suffered the most from the consequences of the pandemic.

<em>Chemin Roxham et Entente sur les tie: Roxham Road and the 2004 Safe Third Country Agreement
<em>‍</em>\nLe parti des écologistes pro: ‍ The Greens propose to repeal the Safe Third Country Agreement between Canada and the United States. Because of this agreement, a person coming from the United States is not allowed to claim asylum at an official border crossing. As a result, many migrants have to enter Canada illegally, and most of them cross at Roxham Road, in Quebec. In 2019, more than 16,000 people were intercepted in the province (out of a total of 16,500 in Canada). Repealing the agreement would therefore allow migrants to arrive in Canada from the United States by a legal and safer route. ‍
<em>‍</em>\nUn des problèmes souvent mon: ‍ One of the problems often pointed to on the immigration file is the discretionary power Canada Border Services Agency officers hold over immigrants. Currently, officers can admit them, refuse them entry into the country, and even place them in immigration holding centres. ‍
‍\nLe Parti vert propose donc de « révis: ‍ The Green Party is therefore proposing to “review all practices of the Canada Border Services Agency,” but also to “put in place an oversight mechanism to remove officers’ discretionary power,” John Chenery, the party’s communications director, explained to us by email. ‍
<em>Les délais de traitement et les trav: Processing times and temporary workers Like all the other parties, the Green Party intends to reduce processing times for asylum and family reunification applications. How? By reviewing immigration requirements and increasing the staff who examine applications, spokesperson John Chenery explained to us. ‍
<em>Et pour ce qui est de l’enjeu des tr: As for the issue of vulnerable temporary foreign workers, it is barely mentioned in the platform. Asked about it, Mr. Chenery did not specify any measures, but noted that workers who want to report abusive working conditions must be protected, not punished, and added that permanent residency must be made more accessible to them. ‍

Connu pour ses positions antiracistes et: Known for its anti-racist positions and its fight against discrimination, Jagmeet Singh’s party seems to make immigration a central issue. In the section on the topic, the party highlights the essential contribution of diversity and immigration to the country, while denouncing the conditions in which immigrants are received and integrated. The NDP proposes to fix the Liberals’ mistakes, but beyond that, its proposals are not very concrete. ‍
Les néo-démocrates comptent eux aussi tr: The New Democrats also intend to strike a balance between addressing the labour shortage and welcoming everyone. Nothing is specified about the details of this middle ground. Jagmeet Singh’s party wants to “improve the recognition of foreign credentials” by the provinces, but does not say how. In Quebec, for example, getting your diplomas and experience recognized can be a laborious process, and many people have to go back to school (often from the beginning) to practise their profession. ‍
Présenté comme « une priorité » pour le:
Presented as “a priority” for the party, family reunification is a process plagued by major delays, which the NDP wants to tackle. “During the COVID-19 pandemic, the department’s offices abroad were closed,” which caused significant delays, Thibault Camara of the group Le Québec c’est nous aussi explained to us. The activist says many families are separated because they cannot obtain a visitor visa to Canada while waiting for family reunification.

‍\nPour les néo-démocrates, le système d: ‍ The New Democrats want to abolish the lottery system currently in place because it is too arbitrary and unfair. In its place, they propose ending the “unfair capping of applications,” which could mean higher thresholds. The lottery had already been scrapped by the Liberals. But after the fiasco of the “first come, first served” model that replaced it, the lottery was reinstated in 2020. For Thibault Camara of Le Québec c’est nous aussi, a group that helps immigrants in Quebec, family reunification is a crucial issue that is talked about far too little in Canada. ‍

Dirigé par Yves-François Blanchet, le Bl: Led by Yves-François Blanchet, the Bloc Québécois is the only party in the race that defends only the interests of Quebec. It has never hidden its indignation at the processing times for immigration applications from Quebec, denouncing Ottawa’s laxity. ‍
Fidèle à ses positions, le Bloc québécoi:
True to its positions, the Bloc Québécois is against the Safe Third Country Agreement in order to stop all irregular crossings into Quebec via Roxham Road. To do so, the party wants “the entire border to be considered an official border crossing.” It also proposes increasing the number of commissioners to speed up the processing of asylum claims and not authorizing any deportations to countries experiencing conflict. As early as 2019, Mr. Blanchet argued that these delays were costing Quebec taxpayers dearly: “It is not up to Quebecers to foot the bill,” he said in September 2019.
‍
Pour un candidat à la résidence permanen: For a permanent residency applicant living in Quebec, processing can take up to 27 months. For a person living elsewhere in Canada, getting an answer from Ottawa takes six months. According to Le Québec c’est nous aussi, this gap affects roughly 56,000 people, which the Bloc firmly denounces. While the platform specifies nothing to correct this delay, communications manager Karine Lafontaine presented four concrete solutions to us by email:
Que les dossiers ne soient plus retourné: Applications should no longer be sent back “as soon as a document is missing.”
« Que les demandes [d’immigration au féd: “Applications [for federal and provincial immigration] should be processed in parallel” rather than in sequence.
Par contre, le Bloc impute uniquement la: However, the Bloc places the blame solely on the federal government, whereas Quebec’s immigration thresholds, which have been lower for a few years, are also a factor, according to the movement Le Québec c’est nous aussi.
En phase avec les demandes du premier mi: In line with Premier François Legault’s demands, the Bloc would like the province to control the “family reunification” category, as well as the Temporary Foreign Worker Program. It hopes this would speed up the processing of applications and allow candidates to be selected based on their command of French. Family reunification accounts for 24% of immigration to Quebec. Finally, the Bloc intends to table a bill making French a condition for obtaining citizenship (a federal responsibility) for applicants living in Quebec. However, it is hard to know whether such a measure is feasible. ‍
<strong>‍</strong>\nLe Parti libéral de: ‍ Justin Trudeau’s Liberal Party kept 52% of the commitments it made in 2019. On immigration, the promises were few: it had promised to modernize the Safe Third Country Agreement, increase immigration and allow permanent residents to apply for citizenship for free. Two years later, of these three major promises, only one has been kept. Applying for Canadian citizenship still costs adults $630, and the Safe Third Country Agreement is still in force. Nothing is planned on this in the current platform. ‍
<em>‍</em>\nRévélées par la pandémie, le: ‍ The living and working conditions of vulnerable temporary foreign workers, laid bare by the pandemic, are not mentioned in the Liberal platform. But Radio-Canada reports in an article that the party plans to improve the measures in place to protect the most vulnerable. ‍
En 2019, un permis de travail ouvert et: In 2019, an open work permit and a complaints system had already been put in place. But according to worker advocacy organizations and immigrants themselves, these measures are hard to access and do not provide real protection. On September 9, the Canadian Council for Refugees (CCR) held a conference to lay out the various shortcomings of these measures. For example, 0.016% of open permit applications are approved, according to the CCR’s study. Organizations like the Migrant Rights Network, which launched an online campaign allowing citizens to write to candidates in the federal election and demand status for all, are still waiting for measures to regularize all essential workers. ‍
<strong>‍</strong>\nDans sa nouvelle pla: ‍ In its new platform, the Liberal Party intends to reduce processing times, which can currently reach 24 months. To make up for these delays, the Liberal Party proposes issuing visas to spouses and children abroad. It is a way to reunite families while they wait for permanent residency. But parents and grandparents are not covered. ‍
<em>‍</em>\nLes libéraux proposent d’ouv: ‍ The Liberals propose opening permanent residency even further to workers and graduates already in Canada. But this would only apply to the Express Entry program, and therefore not to Quebec, at first glance. ‍
Pour ce qui est des réfugiés, le parti v: As for refugees, the party wants to welcome 2,000 of them based on labour needs. However, the document does not specify whether this number is in addition to the 2021–2023 Immigration Plan, which calls for welcoming 421,000 newcomers in 2023, or part of it. It should be added that this measure comes from a pilot project launched in 2018. ‍
<em>‍</em>\nDepuis le début de la crise: ‍ Since the start of the health crisis, processing times for immigration applications have exploded. To catch up on the backlog, made worse by the pandemic, the Liberal Party proposes reducing processing times to 12 months. However, it does not specify which applications are covered, nor what means will be used to achieve this. ‍

Le parti d’Erin O’Toole propose de « rép: Erin O’Toole’s party proposes to “fix the Liberal government’s mistakes” by bringing “order” to the immigration and asylum systems, and to achieve this goal by better enforcing the law. The Conservatives’ measures mostly run counter to those of the other parties. On the other hand, they are the only ones to tackle discrimination and injustice in the issuing of visitor visas. ‍
Les conservateurs proposent d’augmenter: The Conservatives propose increasing the resources of the Immigration and Refugee Board of Canada (IRB) to speed up the review of asylum claims. The IRB is the tribunal that handles asylum claims and the cases of immigrants who have been removed or who have appealed a decision. Again running counter to the other parties, the CPC would like the state to stop being involved in refugee resettlement. Sponsorship (private or joint) would be favoured. ‍
